summary: Describes a MIB-based use of AAA information, such as from RADIUS, to dynamically update user-to-group mappings in the SNMP View-based Access Control Model (VACM).

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices decide who can see what based on groups. This lets the central login system update those group memberships on the fly.

questions: how does radius set snmp access groups
subtitle: Lets a central login server decide which SNMP access group each user belongs to, so devices need no manual updates.

tldr.problem: In SNMP's access control model (VACM), the mapping from each user to an access group is configured by hand on every device, which is a chore when people join, leave or change roles.
tldr.mechanism: A small MIB module records, per authenticated session, the group name that the AAA service (such as RADIUS) supplied. Procedures then create, update or delete the matching VACM user-to-group rows, but only rows marked volatile and active.
tldr.outcome: The AAA server can drive user-to-group assignments without any change to VACM itself. The group's access policy must already exist on the device, so no user can gain rights that VACM has not already granted to some group.

facts.label: Table index
facts.value: Security model, security name, session ID

today: RFC 6065 is a Proposed Standard (December 2010), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to RFC 5607 and RFC 5608.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
The View-based Access Control Model (VACM, RFC 3415) decides who may read or change which management data in SNMP. VACM maps a user to a group, and the group names the access control policy for that user. RFC 6065 describes how to fill in that user-to-group mapping dynamically from an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) service, such as RADIUS (RFC 2865 and RFC 5607).

The goal is to reduce the need for security administrators to update VACM configurations by hand as users come and go. The memo requires no change to the Abstract Service Interface for the Access Control Subsystem and no change to the Elements of Procedure for VACM. It adds a MIB module and procedures for maintaining it and for updating the VACM tables.

Readers are expected to know RFC 3415, RFC 5607 and RFC 5608.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a grown-up has to write down by hand which club each kid belongs to. This idea lets the front desk that already checks everyone in say which club each kid is in.

sections.title: How AAA Fits With SNMP Access Control
sections.content:
The memo handles one of two use cases for AAA with SNMP: access control authorization. (The other, service authorization, is covered in RFC 5608.) The assumption is that roles in an organization, which VACM represents as groups, change rarely, while the users assigned to those roles change often. So the user-to-role mapping is delegated to the RADIUS server.

Detailed access control policies are assumed to be already configured in VACM. The only extra information taken from the AAA service is the mapping of the authenticated user to a group. RADIUS does not separate authentication from authorization the way the SNMP architecture (RFC 3411) does, so the design reuses the RADIUS conventions of RFC 5608 together with the RADIUS Management-Policy-Id Attribute (RFC 5607).

The key concept is an informal AAA binding that ties together a communications channel, an authenticated principal, service authorization and an access control policy name. A transport model such as the Secure Shell Transport Model (RFC 5592) binds the first three, RFC 5607 adds the policy name, and this memo extends the binding to the local VACM definition of that named policy.

The memo may also be used with other transport models and other AAA services, as long as they provide equivalent session start and end indications, a principal identifier that can become an SNMP securityName, and information equivalent to the Management-Policy-Id.
sections.plainLanguage: The school already has rules for what each club may do. The front desk only has to say which club a visitor belongs to, and the rules for that club then apply automatically.

sections.title: The vacmAaaSecurityToGroupTable
sections.content:
The MIB module defines a single table, vacmAaaSecurityToGroupTable. It is indexed by three things: the integer assigned to the security model (vacmAaaSecurityModel), the protocol-independent securityName for the principal (vacmAaaSecurityName), and a unique session identifier (vacmAaaSessionID). The one readable column is vacmAaaGroupName, which in RADIUS environments comes from the Management-Policy-Id Attribute.

Each row corresponds to one session. The session ID must be unique among all currently open sessions of all of the SNMP engine's transport models, and has no other meaning. The security name is a string of 1 to 32 characters, and the security model cannot take the value 0 ("any").

The module is rooted at { mib-2 199 }. It does not change any VACM element of procedure and does not affect any VACM table other than through the procedures in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a visitor log with one line per visit: who came, which door they used, a unique visit number, and which club the front desk said they belong to.

sections.title: Session Start and Session End Procedures
sections.content:
The procedures are driven by two events: a session is established, or a session ends. The handling of a session establishment indication MUST be completed before isAccessAllowed() is invoked for any SNMP PDU from that session. If the session ends before all such invocations finish, the remaining ones MAY be denied.

When a session starts

Four pieces of information are REQUIRED: the security model, the RADIUS User-Name Attribute, a session identifier, and the Management-Policy-Id Attribute. If the User-Name or the Management-Policy-Id is absent, invalid or a zero-length string, nothing more is done.

  • If no matching row exists in vacmAaaSecurityToGroupTable, create one. If it exists, update its vacmAaaGroupName.
  • When a new row is created, look in the regular vacmSecurityToGroupTable for an entry with the same model and name. If none exists, create one with the group name, a StorageType of volatile and a RowStatus of active.
  • When vacmAaaGroupName changes, update the VACM vacmGroupName only if that entry is volatile and active. Otherwise it MUST NOT be modified.

When a session ends

Matching rows (same security model and session ID) are deleted from vacmAaaSecurityToGroupTable. Finding no match is not an error. When the last row for a given model and name pair is removed, the corresponding VACM row is also deleted, but only if it is volatile and active. Rows of the AAA table MUST NOT persist across reboots.

The reasoning for the volatile test is that an entry made by a security administrator would not normally be marked volatile, so a volatile entry was probably created dynamically. Newer information from the AAA service supersedes the group currently held.
sections.plainLanguage: When a visitor arrives, the front desk writes their club on the list, unless a grown-up already wrote something permanent. When the visitor leaves, the front desk erases only the notes it wrote itself.

sections.title: Failure Cases and Sequencing
sections.content:
The memo says there are implementation-dependent error cases it does not spell out, such as running out of memory. Implementors are advised to consider fail-safe strategies: for example, prematurely terminating access is preferred to erroneously perpetuating access.

The procedures also assume that a transport model such as RFC 5592 coordinates session establishment with AAA authentication and authorization, and that the AAA client receives the Management-Policy-Id from the RADIUS Access-Accept message (or equivalent). The User-Name from the Access-Request is assumed to correspond to a securityName.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong, it is safer to send a visitor home too early than to let them stay when they should not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures make a heuristic use of StorageType: they treat non-volatile entries as ones an administrator provisioned, and active volatile entries as dynamic and safe to update or delete. The memo warns that this assumption is reasonable but not universally valid. For example, an administrator could have created non-volatile entries by mistake.

The design of VACM ensures that an unknown group name grants no access. So whatever the AAA server says, no user can gain SNMP access rights that are not already granted to some group in the VACM configuration.

Naming consistency. The identity chain must be consistent. Either the VACM user-to-group entries for a security model are created only by these procedures, or administrators must make sure each pre-configured vacmSecurityName matches the authenticated RADIUS User-Name. Reusing the same name for different people can lead to the wrong policy being applied, with greater or lesser rights than intended, and the SNMP engine may not be able to detect it.

Exposure of the table. The module has no read-write or read-create objects, so SET operations cannot alter it. But walking the table reveals user names, security models, session identifiers and group names, so access to it should be controlled and possibly encrypted. The memo RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of who is in which club is private, so only the right people should be able to read it. And the front desk can only pick from clubs that already exist, so it can never invent a super-powerful one.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The only IANA action is the object identifier for the module, recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: vacmAaaMIB is { mib-2 199 }.

The MIB module itself is called SNMP-VACM-AAA-MIB. It comes from the ISMS Working Group, with an initial revision dated 9 December 2010, and its compliance statement requires the single object group vacmAaaGroup.
sections.plainLanguage: The module gets its own official number so everyone can find it in the same place.
